text: Crestfallen means sad and disappointed, like a bird whose head feathers droop after losing a fight. The camerawoman filming the newsroom's last days is crestfallen because the paper she loves is being closed.

To commemorate is to honour the memory of a person or event with a ceremony or a special day. The publisher was travelling to Paris to mark twenty years since the murder of the reporter Anna Politkovskaya.
Escalation is a step-by-step rise in how serious or dangerous something gets. The break-in and the threat of arrests showed the pressure on the paper was growing, so the staff chose to close.
Modernist describes a style of building from the 20th century with plain shapes, big windows and little decoration.
A printing press is a machine that prints newspapers and books in large numbers. The paper's building was once a place where such machines ran.
Renowned means famous and respected for something, here for being an excellent reporter.
A laureate is someone honoured with a major prize. Dmitry Muratov won the Nobel Peace Prize, so he is a Nobel laureate.
The Nobel Peace Prize is one of the world's most famous awards. Mr Muratov shared it in 2021 for defending freedom of expression.
To evict someone is to force them to leave a building they live or work in, usually by order of an owner or authority.
In Russia, "foreign agent" is an official label for people or groups the state says are influenced from abroad. It brings paperwork, warnings and blocked money, and scares off donors and advertisers.
To detain someone is to hold them under authority, such as the police, without letting them go freely. The editor was detained and questioned.
In Russia, a group declared "extremist" can see its members arrested simply for belonging. The staff feared the paper would be given this label.
To break into a place is to enter it illegally by force. Someone did this to the paper's offices the night before the meeting.
A constitution is a country's basic set of rules about how it is governed and what rights people have.
Article 29 of Russia's constitution promises free speech and says censorship is banned. Mr Muratov mocks it because the state ignores it.
Censorship is when a government or other powerful group controls what can be published or said. Russia's constitution bans it on paper.
Militaristic describes a country that puts armed force and war at the centre of its politics.
A dictatorship is a country ruled by one person or a small group with no real free elections or free press.
To isolate a country is to cut it off from others, here through the sanctions and diplomatic break with the West after the invasion.
A licence is official permission to do something. Russia revoked the paper's licence to publish.
To revoke something is to cancel it officially. The state took back the paper's permission to publish.
Ingenious means clever and inventive. The paper found clever ways to reach readers even after being blocked.
To expose something is to reveal a hidden truth, especially wrongdoing, to the public.
Chechnya is a mostly Muslim region in southern Russia where Russia fought brutal wars in the 1990s and 2000s. Novaya Gazeta's reporting on the violence made it famous.
To secure something is to make it firm or safe. The Chechen war helped Mr Putin make his hold on power firm.
Cynicism is the belief that people act only out of selfishness, and the open disregard for honesty that can follow.
Fascism is a harsh form of government with a powerful dictator, no opposition, and aggressive nationalism.
To be gunned down is to be shot dead, usually in a sudden and violent way.
To treat people like dust means to show no respect for their lives or worth. Mr Muratov says such treatment leads to violence.
To spill beyond a border is to spread outward. His warning is that a government's violence at home often becomes violence abroad.
Donbas is an industrial region in eastern Ukraine where Russia-backed fighting began in 2014.
Separatists want a region to break away from its country. Russia claimed that local rebels, not its army, were fighting in Donbas.
The Wagner group was a private army of mercenaries used by Russia, including in Ukraine and Africa.
A mercenary is a soldier who fights for money rather than for a country.
A mutiny is a rebellion by soldiers against their commanders. Prigozhin led one against Mr Putin in 2023.
Evgeny Prigozhin founded the Wagner group. He led a revolt against Mr Putin and died soon after in a plane crash.
A wreath is a ring of flowers, usually laid at funerals. Sending them to a living person is a threat to say "you will die".
A ram is a male sheep. Sending severed rams' heads to the offices was another frightening threat.
An invasion is when an army enters another country by force. Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
To criminalise something is to make it a crime. Russia made it illegal to call the war a "war".
De facto is Latin for "in fact". It describes something that is true in practice even if it is not officially declared.
A newsstand is a small kiosk on the street that sells newspapers and magazines.
The editorial staff of a paper are the people who write and edit its stories.
Latvia is a small European country on the Baltic Sea next to Russia, where many exiled Russian journalists have settled.
Deterioration means getting worse. The paper reported on Russia's worsening economy as a result of the war.
Trauma is lasting emotional damage after a terrible experience such as war or violence.
Dignity means being treated with respect. The paper gave opponents of the war a place where they felt respected, not alone.
To be hailed as a hero means to be praised publicly. The reporter means a normal world would not do this for people who commit crimes.
To escalate is to make something more intense or severe, like attacks on cities.
To demolish something is to knock it down completely. Here it is used figuratively for destroying free public spaces.
Artefacts are objects made by people that have historical or personal importance, like items from the newsroom.
An accomplice is someone who helps another to commit a crime. Mr Muratov jokingly uses it for readers who helped the paper.
Under Joseph Stalin, who led the Soviet Union until 1953, millions were imprisoned, sent to camps, or killed for political reasons.
Political prisoners are people jailed for their beliefs or opposition to the government rather than for real crimes.
Solovetsky is an island in northern Russia that held one of the first Soviet prison camps.
The gulag was the Soviet system of forced-labour prison camps.
Anna Politkovskaya was a Novaya Gazeta reporter who exposed abuses in Chechnya. She was shot dead in 2006.
Dmitry Muratov is the paper's publisher and a Nobel Peace Prize winner who stayed in Moscow to keep it going.
Novaya Gazeta means "New Newspaper" in Russian. It was Russia's best-known independent paper, founded in 1993.
